beginner.headline: Data Centres in Scotland: Plans and Worries
beginner.brief: Many huge data centres are planned for Scotland. These centres help with online tasks like bank payments or using AI. From the outside, data centres look like a factory. Inside, thousands of computers work and make noise. Supporters say data centres can bring jobs and investment. But opponents worry about the energy they use and their size. Scotland has strong renewable energy, which data centres need. However, some centres might use fossil fuels if there is not enough wind power.

intermediate.headline: Scotland's Data Centre Boom: Investment vs. Environmental Concerns
intermediate.brief: Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes. Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them - on a massive scale. The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new 'hyperscale' data centres. Supporters say they are vital for the future and could bring billions of pounds in investment, as well as thousands of jobs. Opponents fear the impact of their size on local communities, the vast amounts of energy they use and even the noise they will make. If one planned for Chapelcross in Dumfries and Galloway goes ahead, it will have a capacity of 1,000MW, making it one of the largest data centres in the world. The Scottish Greens and campaign groups have called for a moratorium on large data centres, arguing they could undermine climate targets and place additional pressure on renewable energy supplies. The Scottish government has so far refused to impose a moratorium. As well as using huge amounts of electricity, the giant data centres can require large quantities of water to prevent them from overheating. Those behind AI data centres say they will create jobs and offer a stake in a key future technology.

advanced.headline: Scotland's Data Centre Boom: Growth, Controversy, and Environmental Impact
advanced.brief: At least 23 huge data centres are planned in Scotland, causing significant concern for campaigners. Scotland is currently involved in a global race to construct many more of these facilities on a truly immense scale. The rapid rise of artificial intelligence has spurred tech firms to build "hyperscale" data centres, some of which could rank among the largest globally. Supporters claim these centres are crucial for the future, potentially attracting billions in investment and creating thousands of jobs. Conversely, opponents are worried about their immense physical footprint, the vast quantities of electricity and water they consume, and the constant operational drone they might generate. For instance, one proposed 600MW data centre at Auchtertool would encompass an area comparable in size to the entire adjacent village. While Scotland boasts a robust renewable energy sector, experts caution that these facilities might not operate entirely on green power, potentially necessitating fossil fuels during periods of low wind. The UK government has designated Lanarkshire as an AI growth zone, positioning data centres at its heart and projecting £8bn of investment and 3,400 jobs. However, the types of jobs created have been debated, with a substantial portion anticipated in construction rather than directly in AI. Despite calls for a halt from environmental groups, the Scottish government has so far refused to impose a suspension on applications but has mandated environmental impact assessments. Ministers will also need to be notified of any proposed centres exceeding 50MW in capacity, though comprehensive national guidance is still pending.
